title: A Tiny Moon That Voyager Never Saw

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Uranus, the seventh planet from the Sun, is already known for an unusually crowded family of moons and a tilted, tangled system of rings. In February 2025, astronomers added one more member to that family: a small moon so faint that no previous mission had ever recorded it, spotted only because a modern space telescope was powerful enough to catch its dim reflected light.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The discovery was made using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, in a programme led by planetary scientist Maryame El Moutamid of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colorado. On 2 February 2025, Webb's Near-Infrared Camera captured a series of ten long-exposure images, each lasting forty minutes, over a period of roughly six hours, tracking a faint point of light moving against the background of stars in a pattern consistent with an object orbiting Uranus itself. The observations were taken through a wide infrared filter sensitive to wavelengths between one and two and a half microns, well beyond what the human eye can detect, and formed part of a broader Webb research programme open to scientists from around the world who compete for a limited amount of telescope time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The newly found body has been given the provisional designation S/2025 U1. Because it has not been imaged in enough detail to measure directly, its size has to be estimated: assuming it reflects light in a similar way to Uranus's other small moons, astronomers calculate a diameter of about six miles, or ten kilometres, making it one of the smallest moons known anywhere in the solar system.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Its orbit lies roughly 35,000 miles, or 56,000 kilometres, from the centre of Uranus, in the gap between two previously known moons, Ophelia and Bianca. The orbit is nearly circular and lies close to Uranus's equatorial plane, a combination that suggests the moon formed in roughly its present location rather than being captured later from elsewhere in the solar system, as sometimes happens with more distant, irregular satellites.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: With this addition, Uranus's known moon count rises to twenty-nine, and the new object becomes the fourteenth member of its group of small inner moons, a crowd that orbits far closer to the planet than its five largest and best-known satellites, Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon. Following long tradition, Uranus's moons are named not after figures from classical mythology, as is usual elsewhere in the solar system, but after characters drawn from the plays of Shakespeare and the poetry of Alexander Pope; the newcomer's eventual name will still need formal approval from the International Astronomical Union. Even among planetary scientists, keeping track of so many small, closely spaced bodies is a demanding task, since their orbits interact with one another and with the planet's faint rings in ways that are still not fully mapped out.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What makes the find particularly striking is what earlier exploration failed to see. NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft flew past Uranus on 24 January 1986, capturing the only close-up images of the planet's moons that exist to this day, and yet it did not detect this moon at all. Its size simply placed it below the threshold that Voyager's instruments, or any Earth-based telescope in the decades since, could resolve, meaning the moon had been circling Uranus unnoticed for the nearly forty years between that flyby and Webb's observations.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Researchers on the team argue that the discovery is significant precisely because of how crowded and interconnected Uranus's inner system already is. According to team member Matthew Tiscareno of the SETI Institute, no other planet in the solar system has as many small inner moons as Uranus, and the complicated gravitational relationships between these moons and the planet's faint rings point to a chaotic early history, one in which the line between "ring" and "moon" may not always have been as clear as it is today.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: For now, the discovery remains part of ongoing research rather than a finished, peer-reviewed result, but it illustrates a broader pattern in planetary astronomy: each generation of instruments reveals objects that the previous generation's technology, however capable at the time, simply could not see. As El Moutamid noted, the moon is small, but finding something that even a dedicated flyby mission missed underlines how much of even a well-studied planetary system can still remain hidden from view. In that sense, the discovery is as much a tribute to Voyager 2's legacy as a correction of its limits: it is precisely because scientists have spent decades studying the images that spacecraft sent back that they know exactly where, and how carefully, to look with today's far more sensitive instruments.
